title: Designing internal SDKs and public APIs
summary: A good API is small, clear at the call site, hard to misuse, explicit about threading, and has a plan for changes and deprecation.
body: **In simple words:** Write the code your users (other teams) will write first, then design the API that makes that code read clearly.

**Make misuse hard:** use types instead of strings (enums for options, structs for configuration), state threading in the signature (`async`, `@MainActor`, `Sendable`), avoid callbacks on unknown queues.
**Small surface:** everything `internal` by default; `public` is a promise you must keep. Use `package` for cross-module internals. Do not expose third-party types in your signatures.
**Evolution:** semantic versioning; `@available(*, deprecated, renamed:)` with a migration period; library evolution mode if you ship binary XCFrameworks.
**Being a good guest in the host app:** never crash the host, log through an injectable logger, offer a remote kill switch, and document cost (launch time, memory, binary size).
**Naming:** follow the Swift API Design Guidelines - clarity at the point of use, no needless words, methods read like phrases (`list.insert(x, at: 0)`).
keyPoints: Design from call sites; follow Swift API Design Guidelines.
Strong types, explicit isolation, async APIs.
Versioning and deprecation plan; kill switch; never crash the host.
Measure and publish the SDK's cost.

followups: **How do you roll out a breaking change to 30 consuming teams?** Add the new API alongside the old, deprecate with fix-its, provide a codemod/guide, track adoption, remove after a set date.
**Delegate vs closure vs AsyncSequence for SDK events?** AsyncSequence for streams in modern Swift; delegate for many related callbacks; closure for one-off.
